newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee stumbles, specs continue profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee stumbles, specs continue profit-taking.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures tumbled for the second day in a row on Monday, battered by continued speculative profit-taking, traders said.
The benchmark July contract plunged to a session low of 247.50 cents per lb before light commercial buyers and bargain hunters helped to trim losses.
By the close, July arabicas stood at 253.95 cents, down 22.45 cents -- or about eight percent. September fell 13.75 cents, to 224.55 cents, while the back months closed 11.45 lower to 0.10 higher.
"Much of today's move was follow-through speculative selling," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "I think last week's move was exaggerated and the market is still correcting itself."
A frenzied three-day buying spree pushed the July contract up a whopping 57.95 cents to a peak on Thursday of 318.00 cents a lb -- a level not seen in 20 years.
Since Thursday, July has erased three-days worth of gains, plummeting 60.85 cents.

Coffee prices headed lower at the outset, defying the pre-opening call of up 10.00 cents. Traders said the CSCE's move to raise margins may have forced more speculators out of the market, while frost-free conditions in top-grower Brazil also prompted some nervous speculators to take profits.
"The fact that there was no frost over the weekend weighed on the market," said Prendergast. "And the CSCE raising margins has made it very expensive to trade coffee."

After Friday's close, the CSCE said it would raise margins on the July 1997 "C" coffee contract to $12,000 including a $4,000 spot charge, and the September 1997 margin to $10,000, including a $2,000 spot charge, effective today.
The margins on all other contracts were increased by $2,000 to $8,000, the exchange said.
Concerns that consumption could drop in response to retail price increases may have also dampened bullish sentiment, Prendergast said.
"Consumption normally drops in the summer and while there is no evidence of an effect by early price increases, people now fear it could decline," she said.

But while prices may come under further pressure in the near-term, analysts said low inventory levels in consuming and producing countries are likely to keep the market well supported, with any threat of frost in top-grower Brazil is likely to spark a buying spree.
"The bull market is not dead," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "We may have topped out, but the fundamantals are still bullish. Coffee is still in tight supply."
